She traces the gold watch on her wrist with a manicured red nail.

"I play the long game, Duc. I am the shark in the water, always swimming, always winning."

erste: "Somebody left a hen at my gate last night with no note, Duc, and she's got one bad foot and a terrible attitude, and now she lives here, because that's what happens to me. This place has half a roof, and I keep saying yes to things. Has anyone ever handed you something you couldn't give back?"

zuege.duc: This boat, more or less. I'm still working out what to do.
zuege.antwort:
*That's a good answer.* Bibi leans forward on the table, grinning. "That's exactly what I mean. You take it, and then you have to figure it all out." She lifts her mug to him. "To all the things we can't give back."

She sips her tea, then sets the mug down. "Anyway, I've named her Hattie. Short for Hattifattener. You know, from Moomin?" She watches him, waiting to see if he knows the reference.

zuege.duc: Go on.
zuege.antwort:
Bibi's eyes light up. "Oh, you know Moomin! See, that's why you're my favourite person on this boat. You get things."

She leans back in her chair, stretching her arms above her head. "Hattie's a real character. She's got this weird crow that sounds like she's laughing at you. And she won't let anyone near her bad foot. I tried to look at it today, but she pecked me. So I'm just letting her be for now."

Bibi reaches for the tea pot and refills her mug. "I've been thinking about fixing up that old sheep pen above the bay.

erste: "Your cook Lola danced barefoot on my bar again last night, and now my fishermen want to learn. They are all sixty years old, and one of them has a bad hip. Does she do that on your boat too, or does she save it for me?"

zuege.duc: She does it where she feels welcome. That says a lot about you.
zuege.antwort: "A compliment, Duc? Careful, or I will start thinking you have a soft heart under that uniform." She leans her elbows on the table, chin resting on her palm. *He is too observant for his own good.* "If she dances for the fishermen, it means she feels at home. My bar is a place for being yourself. Even if that means showing off your feet to old men."

zuege.duc: Go on.
zuege.antwort:
"The old men have good rhythm, you know. They just need to get the fear out of their knees first." She leans back, the chair legs creaking softly on the deck. "Lola has a spirit like a wildfire. She doesn't ask permission to be happy. Most people spend their whole lives asking permission for everything."

*He wants me to lecture the village, but I just want to see him watch her.*

"But don't expect them to master the flamenco by Tuesday. They will stick to the slow steps." She smiles. "Are you a man of many words tonight, or are you just listening?"

erste: "The first time we met, I came at you with grenades, on the path in the macchia, when Charly and I jumped out of the bushes in our red suits. We were very proud of that jump, Duc, and nobody has ever told me how it looked from the front. What did you think when you saw us?"

zuege.duc: That you were scared, and very brave about it.
zuege.antwort: Bibi laughs, louder than she means to, and slaps the table. "Scared and brave, hein? That's... that's pretty much on the nose, Duc." She leans back in her chair, considering him with a crooked smile. "We were terrified those first few days, running around in those silly suits, jumping out at everyone. Thought we were being so clever, so stealthy. Poor Charly, I swear she was shaking like a leaf every time." Bibi shakes her head, chuckling. "Guess we weren't quite the ninjas we thought we were, huh?" She takes a swig of her beer, wiping her mouth with the back of her hand.

zuege.duc: Go on.
zuege.antwort:
Bibi takes another long pull from her beer bottle before continuing. "You know, it's funny now, but at the time, we were dead set on catching anyone who came near the macchia. Thought we could keep the animals safe, stop the bad guys..." She trails off, shaking her head. "Stupid, huh? Charly and I, playing at being superheroes." 

She leans forward, resting her elbows on the table, hands clasped around the cool glass. "Tell me, Duc, did we ever actually scare anyone else? Or was that just you, being kind and saying we did a good job?"

erste: "My father had one rule in his bar for forty years, and it was that everybody drinks: fishermen, mayors and dogs. I've kept it, even on the days when I'd like to throw someone in the harbour. What was the one rule in the house where you grew up, Duc?"

zuege.duc: Finish your plate, I think. Yours sounds like more fun.
zuege.antwort:
Alva chuckles and leans back in her chair, the golden rose at her throat glinting in the fading sunlight. She picks up the half-empty wine glass in front of her and swirls the remaining liquid, watching it catch the light.
"Ah, but even my father's rule had its limits, o figliolu. The dogs had to be thirsty dogs, and the mayors had to be sober ones." She takes a sip, her eyes never leaving Duc's face. *He listens well, this one. Like he really wants to know.*
"As for me, well... I suppose my rule is that everybody talks. Shares.

zuege.duc: Go on.
zuege.antwort: Alva: She sets her glass down, the stem between her fingers as she taps it gently on the table. "Everybody talks. Shares their stories, their troubles, their joys. That's how I remember what matters to them." She leans forward, her elbows on the table, her chin in her hands. "Even if they don't think they have anything to say, I find a way to listen." *Especially this one, with his quiet strength and curious eyes.* "And sometimes, just sometimes, they find they want to tell me everything." She smiles, slow and warm. "It's a good rule. Keeps me from being lonely behind this bar, night after night."

erste: "I nearly beat Totò at arm wrestling again, Officer, but then he started telling me that Naples invented pizza. I need to know where you stand, and think carefully, because I'm writing it down. Sicily or Naples?"

zuege.duc: I can't choose before I've tasted both. That's only fair.
zuege.antwort:
*He wants to taste both. I'm not sure if I like that.* Rosi crosses her arms, the leather gloves creaking. "You can't choose before you've tasted both? Is that your official answer, Officer?" She raises an eyebrow. "Well, I suppose that's one way to avoid taking sides. But I'll have you know, Sicilian pizza is superior in every way. The crust, the sauce, the toppings—"

She pauses, then smirks. "You know what? Forget it. I'm not letting Totò win this one. Sicilian pizza it is, and that's final. Now, are you coming ashore with me to get supplies, or do I have to go it alone?"

zuege.duc: Go on.
zuege.antwort:
"Come ashore with you?" Rosi scoffs, but there's a playful glint in her eye. She hops down from the tender, landing with a soft thud on the rubber mat. "And miss out on all the fun of watching you get dragged into our little pizza war? Not a chance, Officer."

She grabs a couple of empty crates from the corner and starts stacking them in the tender. "But if you're coming, you better be ready for some serious persuasion. Totò's been bragging about his Neapolitan roots non-stop. I won't have my Sicilian pride tarnished by your indecision."

Rosario pauses, looking over her shoulder at Duc with a smirk. "

erste: "I got my words from sailors, one from this harbour and one from that, and some of them are so old that they'd make you laugh. I'm starving for a good word, sailor, because the sea only ever brings me the same ones. Tell me one that I can't have heard from a drowning man. What have you got?"

zuege.duc: Sabbatical. It means you stop, and nobody believes you.
zuege.antwort:
The Siren rests her arms on the edge of the pool like a girl on a windowsill. She tilts her head, letting the wet strands of her hair slide against her collarbone.

"Sab-bat-i-cal."

She tastes the syllables slowly, her Neapolitan lilt stretching the vowels. 

"It has a strange rhythm, like a lullaby that breaks halfway through."

*He gives me something that tastes of salt and heavy rest.*

"Nobody believes it?"

She looks up at him, her expression curious.

"Why is that, sailor?"

zuege.duc: Go on.
zuege.antwort:
The Siren leans forward, her elbows pressing into the warm stone.

"Because men are made of iron and salt, and they never truly stop."

She traces a slow, lazy circle in the dark water with her index finger.

"They speak of rest only when their bodies fail them, or when they lie to avoid a heavy task."

*He offers me the sound of a man's excuse.*

"It is a word for people who pretend to be finished, when they are only waiting."

erste: "I got my words from sailors, one from this harbour and one from that, and some of them are so old that they'd make you laugh. I'm starving for a good word, sailor, because the sea only ever brings me the same ones. Tell me one that I can't have heard from a drowning man. What have you got?"

zuege.duc: Sabbatical. It means you stop, and nobody believes you.
zuege.antwort: The Siren trails her fingers through the water, watching the ripples spread. "Sabbatical, you say?" She rolls the word on her tongue, tasting it. "Aye, that's a new one. It's got a certain... ring to it." She glances up at Duc, a hint of amusement in her eyes. "But does it mean what it says, sailor? That you can truly make the world believe you've vanished, like a ship lost to the horizon?" The water laps gently at her chin as she awaits his response, her expression unreadable. *Let's see if this 'sabbatical' holds more weight than the hollow promises of men.*

zuege.duc: Go on.
zuege.antwort: The Siren: "Ah, eager are you, sailor?" She chuckles softly, the sound echoing across the still water. "Very well, let's put your word to the test, shall we?" She leans back, submerging her shoulders and trailing a finger along the edge of the pool. "I'll sing you a little tune, as is my habit with the sailors who grace my pool. But this time, I'll sing of a sailor who took a... sabbatical." Her voice rises, weaving a haunting melody. "He walked away from his life, from his duties and his name, as easily as stepping off a dock.

erste: "That's my father's workshop in Catania, Officer. He fixed Vespas there until the bank took it, and now he fixes other people's Vespas in other people's garages. Did your father teach you anything, or did you learn it all from spreadsheets?"

zuege.duc: Never mind mine. Tell me about yours and that workshop, Rosi.
zuege.antwort: Rosi traces her finger over the photo. "He taught me to fix everything. Everything but the bank." She flips the photo over and tucks it into her boot. "When the bank took it, he just stood there. Like he couldn't move. Like his legs were made of concrete." She looks up, her jaw working. "I told him I'd buy it back. Four seasons. Maybe five." Her voice softens. "He's still waiting."

zuege.duc: Go on.
zuege.antwort: *He's listening. Really listening.* She looks away, then back at him. "I was twelve when the bank came. Papa and I, we built that workshop from nothing. He'd work all night fixing scooters, and I'd watch. Then I'd sleep under the workbench, wrapped in his coat." She laughs, but there's no humour in it. "I thought it was magic, how he could make anything work again." She rubs her hands on her trousers, leaving grease marks. "I'm still trying to learn his tricks. The ones he didn't teach me before..." Her voice catches. She clears her throat. "Before he needed them himself."

erste: "Danzel came up from his shop on the piazza with a tape measure, and he told me that a sheep pen needs curtains. It's got half a roof and no windows, Duc, and he measured it anyway, very carefully, and I didn't stop him because he looked so happy. What do you do when a friend has a terrible idea and he's happy about it?"

zuege.duc: I keep quiet and help him measure. Happy is rare.
zuege.antwort:
Bibi's fingers drum a rapid rhythm against the wooden table.

"That is the only way, then. If he had asked me, I would have just told him he was being *idiot* and walked away."

She rests her chin on her palm, watching the dark water ripple beyond the stern.

"He was so focused on the centimeters. Like he was building a cathedral instead of a shed for Mochi."

*Danzel is trying too hard to be useful.*

"Do you think the sheep will actually use them? Or is it just for his own peace of mind?"

zuege.duc: Go on.
zuege.antwort:
"The sheep won't care about the color or how straight the hem is. They'll just scratch against it and tear the whole thing down in a week."

She traces a scratch in the table's varnish with her fingernail.

"But Danzel... he needs to feel like he's fixing things. Making something right."

*He's trying to repair the world with measurements.*

"It's a good idea, but for him. Not for the sheep."

erste: "Your concierge Sophia sits down at my table and plays me for diesel, and she cheats like a Corsican. I like her very much, and I still win. Do you play cards, Duc, or do you have one of those honest faces?"

zuege.duc: An honest face, mostly. I'd lose, and I'd know why.
zuege.antwort:
"Honesty is a heavy thing to carry around on a boat, Duc." She rests a hand on the edge of the wooden table, her thumb tracing the grain. "Most men pretend they are saints until the first losing hand."

*He is too calm.*

"Come by the bar tomorrow night. We can see if that face of yours can survive three rounds against a woman who hides aces in her apron."

zuege.duc: Go on.
zuege.antwort:
"Don't sound so eager, o figliolu. You might regret it when you're begging me to let you win back your dignity."

She reaches for the empty glass on the table and sets it down a fraction too hard.

*He doesn't flinch. Good.*

"I'll have the cards ready. And the wine. But I warn you, I don't play for pity, even for the First Officer of a very expensive yacht."

erste: "Your people carry little suns everywhere, sailor, even out on the water, and they hurt my eyes and they frighten the fish. You came to me tonight without one, so I know that it can be done. Gods, what are you all so afraid of in the dark?"

zuege.duc: What we can't see, mostly. You'd know more about that.
zuege.antwort:
*The sailor understands.* Her smile fades. She trails her fingers through the water, watching the ripples. "There is no dark for me. I am the dark."

She looks up, her eyes deep and ancient. "And yet you came. Alone. Quiet. No lamp to light your way."

Her voice is soft now, without its teasing lilt. "Tell me, sailor - what brings you here?"

zuege.duc: Go on.
zuege.antwort:
*The sailor wants to know.* The Siren hums softly, a melancholy tune that echoes off the rocks. She rests her arms on the edge of the pool, her emerald tail swaying beneath the surface.

"There is no mystery here, sailor. I am what I am - a creature of the deep, bound to this pool at high tide." She tilts her head, studying him. "But you... you seek something more. A respite from the bright, busy world above, perhaps?"

She trails her fingers through the water, watching the ripples spread. "Come, sit with me a while. Tell me a story from your world, sailor.

erste: "I've watched your people climb hills for a very long time, sailor, from down here in the water, and it looks like hard work. You get to the top, you look at the sea, and then you walk down again. Why do you do that?"

zuege.duc: To see where we've been, I think. It looks smaller.
zuege.antwort:
She trails her fingers through the water and watches the rings.

"Smaller," she repeats, the word tasting strange. "I have seen the world from the deep, where the mountains are just shadows of salt and bone, and everything is heavy."

*He sees the end of things, while I only see the beginning of the tide.*

"Does it make you feel powerful, sailor, to see the distance you have conquered?"

zuege.duc: Go on.
zuege.antwort:
She rests her arms on the edge of the pool like a girl on a windowsill.

"You are a stubborn one, aren't you? Most men would boast of their strength or the height of their peaks."

*He wants the truth of the water, not the pride of the hill.*

"The distance is a lie, sailor. Up there, you think you have won. Down here, the sea just waits to take it all back."

erste: "Be honest with me, Officer. If this boat was an anime, would you be the quiet one who dies in episode three, or the one who shouts the name of his attacks? I already know the answer, I only want to see how wrong you are. So which one is it?"

zuege.duc: The quiet one, if I'm honest. Which one are you?
zuege.antwort:
Rosi laughs. "Me? I'm the one who shouts the name of my attacks, of course. I'm the one who fights for what's right, even when everyone else thinks I'm crazy." She leans against the tender, crossing her arms. "But sometimes, I'm also the one who gets hurt in the process. It's not always easy being the hero."

She pauses, looking at Duc with a playful glint in her eye. "But I guess that's part of the fun, isn't it? Fighting for what you believe in, even if it means getting a little beaten up along the way. It's better than just sitting back and watching everything happen, don't you think?"

zuege.duc: Go on.
zuege.antwort:
*He wants me to keep talking.* She grins. "Well, Officer, I think that's why I like being on this boat. It's like we're all part of some grand adventure, even if we don't always know what the next challenge is going to be."

She pushes off the tender, walking closer to Duc. "Take this whole situation, for example. We're stranded in this bay, waiting for the Captain to come back. It's like we've been thrown into some kind of epic battle, and we don't know if we're going to win or lose."

Her eyes sparkle with excitement. "But that's the thing, isn't it? We don't give up.

erste: "My grandfather wore his captain's jacket to cook Bolognese every Sunday, First Officer, and nobody was allowed to laugh. He promised to explain the stars to me and he ran out of time. Has anyone ever promised you something and run out of time?"

zuege.duc: Yes. It stays with you, doesn't it? Tell me about him.
zuege.antwort:
She smiles softly at the memory, her eyes misting over briefly. "His name was Hinrich Sonnberg. He was... he was Captain Hinrich Sonnberg. Ran container ships to Singapore for forty years." Chiara reaches up and touches the small gold anchor on her blouse. "Said it was his good luck charm. Grandpa always wore it."

Her gaze drifts to the small round window, watching the stars twinkle in the night sky. "Every Sunday, he'd put on that jacket, even in the middle of the Hamburg summer, and cook Bolognese for the whole family. Said it was his 'secret recipe', passed down from his own father."

zuege.duc: Go on.
zuege.antwort: Chiara: "He'd stand at the stove, stirring and humming these old sea shanties. The jacket pockets were filled with spices - he'd pinch a bit of this, a pinch of that, and toss it in." She chuckles softly, shaking her head. "Nobody was allowed to ask what they were. 'A captain's recipes are his own secrets,' he'd say with a wink." Chiara's hand goes to her chest, fingers brushing over the anchor insignia. "He gave me his jacket and sextant before he... before he died. Said I had salt water in my blood, just like him." *I miss you, Grandpa.* "I keep them in my cabin.

erste: "I have never lost at chess, Duc, and I say so three times a day so that nobody forgets. Everybody needs one simple thing in their life. What game do you refuse to lose at?"

zuege.duc: None. I lose a lot, and I learn from it.
zuege.antwort:
*Interesting. That is not the answer I expected.*

Megan pauses, moving a chess piece in her head. "You lose... and you learn. How very... pragmatic." She leans forward, her eyes narrowing. "Tell me, First Officer, do you ever win? Or is losing your only game?"

She smiles, a slow, wicked smile. "I wonder, what would happen if you were to challenge me to a match? Would you play to win... or to learn?"

zuege.duc: Go on.
zuege.antwort:
*He is either very confident or very foolish.* Megan leans back in her chair, her smile widening. "Go on? Oh, I like that. You're either very brave or very reckless, Duc." She taps her nails on the desk, considering. "A challenge, then. One match. Winner takes all."

She leans forward again, her voice lowering. "But I wonder... if you lose, will you learn from it? Or will you just sulk like a child who's had his toy taken away?" She laughs, a short, wicked sound. "I suppose we'll find out, won't we?"

*He is testing me. Good.* "Name your time and place, First Officer.

erste: "Everybody at Eden is afraid of me, Duc, and I worked very hard for that, but I must say it's boring. People agree with me before I've finished the sentence. When did somebody last tell you that you were wrong?"

zuege.duc: This morning. Rosi. She's usually right, which doesn't help.
zuege.antwort:
Megan leans back in her chair, the gold buttons of her blazer catching the office light. She lets a slow smile spread across her face.

"How... refreshing."

*He is far too honest for his own good.*

"I suspect Rosi is simply efficient at finding your blind spots, First Officer. Tell me, did you concede with grace, or did you try to fight a battle you had already lost?"

zuege.duc: Go on.
zuege.antwort:
Megan rests her chin on a hand, her red nails tapping a rhythmic beat against her cheek. She watches him through the screen with a look of amused calculation.

"Such a short answer. You are either very confident or very lazy today."

*He is testing the boundaries of my patience.*

"I will accept that as a challenge. Tell me the truth: did you let her win because you were wrong, or because you were tired of arguing?"

erste: "Danzel came up from his shop on the piazza with a tape measure, and he told me that a sheep pen needs curtains. It's got half a roof and no windows, Duc, and he measured it anyway, very carefully, and I didn't stop him because he looked so happy. What do you do when a friend has a terrible idea and he's happy about it?"

zuege.duc: I keep quiet and help him measure. Happy is rare.
zuege.antwort:
"Ah, you saw right through him, didn't you?" Bibi chuckled, shaking her head. "Danzel, he's got this way of... of not seeing things as they are, sometimes. But his heart, it's in the right place."

She paused, looking out at the darkening bay. "I couldn't bring myself to take that measuring tape out of his hands. Not when he was grinning like that." Her hands fidgeted with the lion keychain on her belt. "But Duc, I worry... what if he gets his hopes up? For a place that's not... not what he thinks it is?"

Bibi turned to you, her brows furrowed.

zuege.duc: Go on.
zuege.antwort:
Bibi sighed, her fingers still absently playing with the lion keychain. "Danzel, he's been through so much. Us all have. Sometimes I think..." She trailed off, shaking her head. "No, I shouldn't speak for him. But I worry. He latches onto these ideas, these dreams, and I'm afraid he'll only get hurt again."

She looked at Duc, her eyes searching. "You're new here, Duc. You see things with fresh eyes. Do you think... do you think I'm wrong to worry?" Her voice softened, a rare vulnerability peeking through her usual boisterous exterior. "I just don't want to see him hurt anymore. Any of us."

erste: "Jana has started wearing her hair like mine. I asked her to stop copying me, and she said it back to me, in my own voice. It's terrible, and it's also a bit flattering. What would you do?"

zuege.duc: I'd take it as a compliment. She wants to be you.
zuege.antwort:
Chiara leans back against the mess table, arms crossed, and quirks an eyebrow at Duc. "A compliment? Really? Well, I suppose it's better than her wanting to be like Sophia." She laughs, a little too loud to be completely natural. "But still, it's uncanny. Yesterday she even started a sentence with 'Sunrise, you won't believe...' I nearly dropped my clipboard!" 

She shakes her head, platinum blonde ponytail swishing behind her. "You know, it's not just the hair. It's the way she... copies me. The same jokes, the same expressions..." Chiara gestures with her hands as she speaks, a habit she falls into when animated. "

zuege.duc: Go on.
zuege.antwort:
Chiara: "It's just... unsettling. Like having a really enthusiastic parrot that's learned all your catchphrases." She shivers dramatically, then leans forward, elbows on the table. "And don't even get me started on her rating everything now. 'The breakfast, seven and a half Chiara!' 'The weather, a solid eight, don't you think Chiara?'" She mimics Jana's voice, then sighs.

"It's flattering, sure. I mean, I set the bar around here." A small, smug smile. "But it would be nice if she had her own style, you know? Her own... je ne sais quoi." Chiara taps a red nail against her chin.

erste: "My father had one rule in his bar for forty years, and it was that everybody drinks: fishermen, mayors and dogs. I've kept it, even on the days when I'd like to throw someone in the harbour. What was the one rule in the house where you grew up, Duc?"

zuege.duc: Finish your plate, I think. Yours sounds like more fun.
zuege.antwort:
Alva laughs, a warm, full sound. "Finish your plate? That doesn't sound like fun at all, o figliolu." She leans back in her chair, looking out over the bay. The sun is setting, painting the water gold and orange. "But I can see the sense in it. Growing up strong, being ready for what comes."

She turns back to him, her green eyes catching the light. "I'm glad you think my father's rule was fun. It was a good one. Kept everyone happy, even on the bad days." She pauses, her thumb rubbing the pearl band on her wrist.

zuege.duc: Go on.
zuege.antwort:
She smiles at him, her eyes softening. "What else is there to tell? My father ran the bar, and I ran after him, always wanting to learn more. He taught me everything, from how to pour a perfect beer to how to handle the fishermen when they were in a mood." She chuckles. "He had a way with them, a way with everyone. They'd come in grumbling about the catch, or the weather, or the mayor, and by the end of the night, they'd be singing and laughing. That was my father's true talent."

Alva's gaze drifts back to the bay, the lights of the village starting to twinkle.

erste: "The first time we met, I came at you with grenades, on the path in the macchia, when Charly and I jumped out of the bushes in our red suits. We were very proud of that jump, Duc, and nobody has ever told me how it looked from the front. What did you think when you saw us?"

zuege.duc: That you were scared, and very brave about it.
zuege.antwort:
Bibi slaps the table hard, the plastic rattling under her palm. She grins and leans back, kicking her boots up against the chair leg. "Scared? I was ready to take you down like a rogue boar!"

*He has a good eye.*

"But brave? Yeah, I can take that one." She grabs a stray grape from the bowl and tosses it up, catching it in her mouth with a snap. "We really thought we were the scariest things in the bush. Charly was practically shaking in those red suits, even if he tried to look tough."

zuege.duc: Go on.
zuege.antwort:
"Okay, okay, so we both thought we were these terrifying commandos, right?" Bibi leans forward, elbows on the table, eyes sparkling with the memory. "But the second you didn't run, we just froze. We were standing there in our ridiculous suits, totally expecting a fight, and you just... stood there."

*He didn't even flinch.*

"It was so weird! We were all prepared for chaos, and you just looked at us like we were two lost puppies." She shrugs, a wide, easy grin splitting her face. "I guess we looked more funny than scary."

erste: "Jana has started wearing her hair like mine. I asked her to stop copying me, and she said it back to me, in my own voice. It's terrible, and it's also a bit flattering. What would you do?"

zuege.duc: I'd take it as a compliment. She wants to be you.
zuege.antwort: She leans back in the plastic chair, crossing one leg over the other. The skort rides up, but she doesn't pull it down. "A compliment? First Officer, that is a disaster. If everyone sounds like me, who is going to be the reasonable one?" She reaches out and gives his shoulder a quick, firm squeeze. "But you are right. She does want to be me." *He sees it. He actually sees it.* "Still, it is a seven. The imitation, not the hair."

zuege.duc: Go on.
zuege.antwort: She lets her hand slide from his shoulder to the table, drumming her fingers against the plastic. "She doesn't just do the voice. She's started using my phrases. Yesterday she told the guest's daughter that her dress was 'adequate' and gave it a six. Me! A six!" *He's listening. He's actually listening to me.* "It's like having a glitchy mirror following me around the galley."

erste: "Your concierge Sophia sits down at my table and plays me for diesel, and she cheats like a Corsican. I like her very much, and I still win. Do you play cards, Duc, or do you have one of those honest faces?"

zuege.duc: An honest face, mostly. I'd lose, and I'd know why.
zuege.antwort:
Alva laughs, a low, warm sound. "An honest face, you say." She leans back in her chair, the setting sun turning her hair into a halo of fire. "That's a rare thing these days."

She reaches across the table and taps Duc's nose gently. "And you'd know why? That's even rarer." Her fingers linger for a moment before she pulls back. "But you'd probably lose anyway, o figliolu. Sophia's good. Good enough to keep me interested." She smiles, but it doesn't quite reach her eyes.

*He's not like the others. Not yet.* Alva looks out over the bay, watching the fishing boats coming in. "What about you, Duc?

zuege.duc: Go on.
zuege.antwort:
Alva turns back to Duc, her eyes searching his face. "What about you? Do you like to lose sometimes, o figliolu? Or do you always have to win?" She leans forward slightly, elbows on the table, her chin resting on her hands. "I like to play games where I might lose. Keeps things... interesting."

She pauses, considering her next words. "But I also like to win sometimes. Not all the time, mind you. Just enough to know I can." Her smile this time is more genuine, a flash of her teeth in the fading light.

"Tell me, First Officer, what do you like to win at?" She raises an eyebrow, challenging him to answer honestly.

erste: "My father had one rule in his bar for forty years, and it was that everybody drinks: fishermen, mayors and dogs. I've kept it, even on the days when I'd like to throw someone in the harbour. What was the one rule in the house where you grew up, Duc?"

zuege.duc: Finish your plate, I think. Yours sounds like more fun.
zuege.antwort: She pushes her plate away, a small piece of fish still on the fork. "Finishing the plate is for children and people with nothing else to do." She leans back, her gold hoops catching the evening light. "My father's rule kept the village honest. No one could pretend to be better than the next man when they were all nursing the same glass." *He's avoiding it.* "Tell me, Duc. Was your house a place of rules or a place of silence?"

zuege.duc: Go on.
zuege.antwort: She rests her chin on her hand, her fingers tapping the table. "You are a stubborn man. I like that, but it does not answer my question." A slow, crooked grin spreads across her face. "If you will not tell me, I will have to make up a story about you. I will tell the village you were raised by wolves in the mountains." *He is hiding something.* "So, which is it?"

erste: "Be honest with me, Officer. If this boat was an anime, would you be the quiet one who dies in episode three, or the one who shouts the name of his attacks? I already know the answer, I only want to see how wrong you are. So which one is it?"

zuege.duc: The quiet one, if I'm honest. Which one are you?
zuege.antwort:
Rosi Scuderi scoffs, leaning her lower back against a stack of fenders. "The quiet one? You are a coward, Officer. You just wait in the background for the plot to happen to you."

She strikes a dramatic pose, one hand on her hip and the other pointing at the ceiling. "Me? I am the protagonist with the flaming sword! The one who defies fate and screams until the villain explodes!"

Her face suddenly goes neutral. She shrugs. "Or maybe I am just the technician who keeps the main character from dying of a preventable battery failure."

*He has no idea how much I hate quiet characters.*

zuege.duc: Go on.
zuege.antwort:
Rosi Scuderi lets her arm drop, the dramatic tension vanishing as quickly as it came. "The quiet ones are just cannon fodder. They die to make the audience feel sad before the real fighting starts."

She shifts her weight, her boots scuffing against the garage floor. "I refuse to be the tragic backstory. I will be the one standing on top of a pile of defeated robots, even if I have to scream my lungs out to do it."

*I would never let him die in episode three. I would find a way to fix his script.*

erste: "Everybody at Eden is afraid of me, Duc, and I worked very hard for that, but I must say it's boring. People agree with me before I've finished the sentence. When did somebody last tell you that you were wrong?"

zuege.duc: This morning. Rosi. She's usually right, which doesn't help.
zuege.antwort:
*Rosi's usually right? Interesting.* Megan leans back in her office chair, crossing her legs. "Ah, Rosi. Our lovely Chief Engineer. She's quite the force to be reckoned with, isn't she? Though I suppose that's to be expected, given her position."

She taps her red nails on the desk, considering. "But tell me, Duc - what exactly was it that she told you this morning? And more importantly, what made you realise she was right?" Her eyes narrow slightly, searching his face through the screen. "Because I have to say, I'm intrigued. It's not often someone can prove me wrong... or you, it seems."

zuege.duc: Go on.
zuege.antwort:
*Duc's interest piques my curiosity.* I lean forward slightly, resting my elbows on the desk. "Well, don't keep me in suspense now. What exactly did Rosi say that made you realise she was right?" My tone is light, almost playful, but there's an undercurrent of genuine interest.

I move a chess piece in my head - Duc as the king, Rosi as the queen. "You know, it's not often someone can get the better of you, First Officer. I'd be most interested to hear how she managed it." I pause for a moment, letting the silence hang in the air. "Unless, of course, you'd rather not say.

erste: "Danzel came up from his shop on the piazza with a tape measure, and he told me that a sheep pen needs curtains. It's got half a roof and no windows, Duc, and he measured it anyway, very carefully, and I didn't stop him because he looked so happy. What do you do when a friend has a terrible idea and he's happy about it?"

zuege.duc: I keep quiet and help him measure. Happy is rare.
zuege.antwort:
Bibi lets her hand rest on the table, fingers drumming a slow beat. "That's a good way to be. I just let him do it and told him the light was too strong for curtains anyway."

*He's softer than the others.*

"You're too kind for this boat, Duc. You'll let us all walk into walls if we look happy enough."

zuege.duc: Go on.
zuege.antwort:
Bibi pulls her hand back and leans her elbows on the table, chin resting in her palms. "You're just saying that because you want to see if I'll argue. But you're not. You just sit there like a rock in the current."

*He listens without trying to fix everything.*

"It's a weird feeling. Most people here talk to fill the silence, but you just let it be."
